elements.label: text
elements.text: Recent breakthroughs in artificial intelligence (AI) are increasingly driven by systems orchestrating multiple large language models (LLMs) and other specialized tools, such as search engines and simulators. So far, these systems are primarily handcrafted by domain experts and tweaked through heuristics rather than being automatically optimized, presenting a substantial challenge to accelerating progress. The development of artificial neural networks faced a similar challenge until backpropagation and automatic differentiation transformed the field by making optimization turnkey. Analogously, here we introduce TextGrad, a versatile framework that performs optimization by backpropagating LLM-generated feedback to improve AI systems. By leveraging natural language feedback to critique and suggest improvements to any part of a system-from prompts to outputs such as molecules or treatment plans-TextGrad enables the automatic optimization of generative AI systems across diverse tasks. We demonstrate TextGrad's generality and effectiveness through studies in solving PhD-level science problems, optimizing plans for radiotherapy treatments, designing molecules with specific properties, coding, and optimizing agentic systems. TextGrad empowers scientists and engineers to easily develop impactful generative AI systems.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Large language models (LLMs) are transforming how breakthrough artificial intelligence (AI) systems are built 1 . The new generation of AI applications increasingly operate as compound systems, orchestrating multiple sophisticated components-from LLM-based agents to specialized tools such as simulators and web search engines. For instance, a system of LLMs communicating with symbolic solvers can solve olympiad-level maths problems 2 ; and a system of LLMs using search engines and code interpreter tools performs comparably to human competitive programmers 3 and solves real-world GitHub issues 4 . Despite these advances, many of these breakthroughs came from systems that are handcrafted by domain experts. Therefore, developing automated optimization algorithms is one of the most crucial challenges to build compound systems with LLMs and accelerate future breakthroughs 5-7 .

elements.label: text
elements.text: For the past 15 years, many advances in AI have relied on neural networks and differentiable optimization 8-12 . Components of neural networks (for example, two artificial neurons) communicate through differentiable functions such as matrix multiplications 13 . Therefore, communicating numerical gradients through each component by backpropagation 14 , which provides the direction to adjust each parameter to improve a model, has been the natural way to train AI models. However, differential optimization does not work easily for the new generation of generative AI systems because these systems often involve natural language interactions, black-box LLMs or external tools, making backpropagating of numerical gradients difficult.

elements.label: text
elements.text: To address this challenge, we introduce TextGrad to perform automatic 'differentiation' via text. While neural networks communicate through numerical values, modern AI systems communicate through unstructured data such as text, code, and images. In TextGrad, each AI system is transformed into a computation graph where components exchange these rich, unstructured variables through complex (not necessarily differentiable) functions. We use 'differentiation' as a metaphor, where LLMs provide feedback (dubbed 'textual gradients' 15 ) in the form of informative and interpretable natural language critiques, describing how each variable should be modified to improve the overall system. Textual gradients are propagated through arbitrary functions, such as LLM application-programming-interface (API) calls, simulators or external numerical solvers. Notably, the text feedback does not target the parameters of the underlying neural networks, and is thus compatible with black-box APIs.

elements.label: text
elements.text: We demonstrate the power of TextGrad in diverse domains, ranging from question-answering benchmarks to radiotherapy treatment plan optimization and molecule generation (Fig. 1), all with a single framework without modifications for different tasks. LLMs can provide rich, legible and expressive natural language feedback to variables in this wide range of domains, such as proposing modifications to molecules, prompts to other LLMs and code snippets. Our framework is built on the premise that current state-of-the-art LLMs can reason about individual components and subtasks of the system that they optimize. Our results demonstrate the promise of TextGrad to automatically improve generative AI systems and its outputs.

elements.text: In traditional automatic differentiation, we compute gradients using the chain rule to determine how to modify the numerical variables in a system to improve the system with respect to an objective function. In comparison, TextGrad generates feedback in the form of text to guide the modifications of unstructured variables in a system. It does not compute numerical gradients, but rather provides critiques suggesting specific modifications that would improve the system with respect to an objective function.

elements.label: text
elements.text: We use TextGrad to solve two broad categories of tasks. First, in test-time optimization, we directly treat a solution to a problem-for example, a code snippet, the solution to a question or a molecule-as an optimization variable. For instance, in the above question-answering objective function, we have a solution that we would like to improve at test time. Our framework produces the textual gradients for and iteratively improves the solution variable. Second, in prompt optimization, the goal is to find a prompt that improves the performance of an LLM in multiple queries for a task. For example, we may want to find a system prompt to an LLM that improves the performance on mathematical reasoning questions. In particular, we want the system prompt to generalize to work for new problems, in contrast to test-time optimization where the only goal is to improve a variable for the problem at hand at test time. Crucially, both types of problem are solved without handcrafting the framework.

elements.label: text
elements.text: We demonstrate the flexibility of TextGrad in a diverse array of applications. First, we optimize code snippets to solve hard problems from LeetCode, an online programming learning platform. Next, we optimize solutions to scientific questions. Third, we optimize prompts to guide the reasoning of LLMs. Fourth, we optimize radiotherapy treatment plans for patients with prostate cancer. Finally, we optimize compound systems involving multiple variables and longer chains. Furthermore, in Supplementary Note 8.1, we discuss how we optimize chemical structures for molecular property maximization as a case study. Across a dataset of 58 target proteins, TextGrad shows improved performance in ligand design compared with alternative molecule optimization methods (Extended Data Figs. 1 and 2).

elements.text: Code optimization

elements.label: text
elements.text: In code optimization, the goal is to modify a code to improve its correctness or runtime complexity. We often have a computation graph like the following:

elements.label: code
elements.text: Refinement objective = LLM (Problem + Code + Test-time instruction + Test results),

elements.label: text
elements.text: where we optimize the code to solve a given problem with limited, local unit-test supervision, and self-evaluation through a test instruction asking to critique the current iteration of the code. Figure 1e shows an example problem: "You are given an array nums of size n consisting of distinct integers from 1 to n and a positive integer k. Return the number of non-empty subarrays in nums that have a median equal to k". The first solution proposed by gpt-4o does not pass the tests. TextGrad identifies an edge case in the first solution and provides a suggestion on how to improve it. The optimized implementation passes all tests.

elements.label: text
elements.text: We use the LeetCode Hard dataset 23 to benchmark code optimization. LeetCode is an online platform that offers coding practice questions in preparation for technical interviews. The dataset contains examples of hard coding problems that are challenging for both humans and language models, where the success metric is completion rate (passing all test cases).

elements.label: text
elements.text: In LeetCode Hard, using gpt-4o in a zero-shot setting gets a 26% completion rate, whereas Reflexion 23 , a state-of-the-art self-refinement baseline, gets a 31% completion rate (Extended Data Fig. 3). With TextGrad, we achieve a completion rate of 36%. These improvements are more significant considering that Reflexion was run with in-context demonstrations and TextGrad did not use any demonstrations (that is, zero shot). We provide more details around the dataset, baselines and prompts in Supplementary Note 3.

In each iteration, the LLM is prompted with the question, current solution and a test-time instruction asking to critique the current iteration. Although an LLM may not get the solution to a problem right at the first attempt, it can improve the solution through iterative refinement 19,23 .

elements.label: text
elements.text: We explore solution optimization in question-answering datasets. We use Google-proof Question Answering (GPQA) 24 , a recent benchmark where multiple-choice questions in physics, biology and chemistry are created and labelled by domain experts who have or are pursuing PhD degrees; two challenging subsets (machine learning and college physics) of the Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) 25 question-answering benchmark that is used to track the progress of language modelling with undergraduate-level questions; MathVista 26 and ScienceQA 27 to test the visual question-answering ability in scientific domains.

elements.label: text
elements.text: With TextGrad, we improve the performance of gpt-4o across these benchmarks (Extended Data Fig. 4a). We improve the performance in MMLU subsets from 85.7% to 88.4% (machine learning) and from 91.2% to 95.1% (college physics), and GPQA from 51.0% to 55.0%. For multimodal reasoning tasks, compared with Reflexion, TextGrad achieves performance gains of 2.1% and 2.2% on MathVista and ScienceQA-IMG (the multimodal setting of ScienceQA). We provide further details in Supplementary Note 4.

elements.text: Prompt optimization for reasoning

elements.label: text
elements.text: LLMs show impressive performance in reasoning tasks, but their performance can be sensitive to the prompt used to guide their behaviour. With the right prompt, their reasoning can be significantly improved 28 . In prompt optimization, the goal is to find a prompt to guide the behaviour of an LLM such that it performs well on a given task. Often, we have a computation graph like the following:

elements.label: text
elements.text: where we have a question, an answer to the question, and an evaluation indicating the quality of the output given the ground-truth answer. For instance, for a question-answering task, the evaluation metric could be the accuracy of the answer.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Here, given a handful of training examples to optimize a prompt, the goal is to maximize the performance of an LLM on the given task.

elements.label: text
elements.text: In our experiments, our goal is to improve the performance of a weaker and cheaper model (for example, gpt-3.5-turbo) using the feedback generated by stronger models (for example, gpt-4o). This task is useful in practice because after paying a fixed cost to optimize a prompt, the prompt-optimized weaker model can be used with cheaper inference costs instead of the stronger and more expensive model. Notably, we can decompose a prompt into instruction and in-context examples 1 , and apply the same strategy to optimize them jointly using textual gradients. For instance, we can initialize the in-context examples using input-output samples from the training dataset, then optimize them using TGD.

elements.label: text
elements.text: We use two standard reasoning tasks (object counting and word sorting) from Big Bench Hard 29 and the GSM8k grade-school maths problem-solving dataset 30 . Across the three datasets, TextGrad improves the performance of the zero-shot prompt (Extended Data Fig. 5a). TextGrad outperforms OPRO 31 , performs similarly to the state-of-the-art prompt optimization framework DSPy 5 for word sorting and GSM8k, and improves over it by 7.0% for object counting. We report ablations in Supplementary Table 1, finding that (1) jointly optimizing demonstrations and the instruction in a prompt improves the performance the most, and (2) optimizing the instruction alone still outperforms other existing methods. We provide examples of optimized instructions and demonstrations in Extended Data Fig. 5.

elements.label: text
elements.text: We perform further ablations to analyse the scalability and robustness of TextGrad. In Supplementary Note 6.1, we perform optimization using Llama-3.1-70B 32 , finding that optimizing the prompts using TextGrad for less capable open-source models is also effective. In Supplementary Note 6.2, we study the robustness of the optimized prompts, finding that prompts optimized for gpt-3.5-turbo can be transferred to open-source models such as Qwen-2.5 33 and Llama-3.2-9B 32 to improve their performance. Finally, in Supplementary Note 6.3, we study the cost-accuracy frontier of the methods, finding that TextGrad brings Pareto improvements.

elements.text: Radiotherapy treatment plan optimization

elements.label: text
elements.text: Radiotherapy is a cancer treatment that uses beams of intense energy, such as X-rays, to kill cancer cells. Before treatment, a team of radiation oncologists and planners collaborate to design an effective treatment plan. This involves determining the necessary dose of radiotherapy and pinpointing the exact locations that need treatment.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Treatment planning involves essentially a two-loop multi-objective optimization problem, where the inner loop aims to optimize the radiation dose delivery to the tumour (planning target volume (PTV)) while protecting healthy organs (organs at risk (OARs)), given the importance weights. The outer loop optimizes these importance weights to trade-off treatment effectiveness with protection. The main challenge lies in translating clinical goals into the weighted objective function. Currently, planners rely on time-consuming trial-and-error approaches to adjust importance weights, making the process time-consuming and costly 34,35 .

elements.label: text
elements.text: We apply TextGrad to perform the outer loop optimization. We perform this optimization at test time with gpt-4o over the importance weights represented as a string, for example, θ = "weight for PTV: [PTV WEIGHT], weight for bladder: [BLADDER WEIGHT], weight for rectum: [RECTUM WEIGHT], weight for femoral heads: [FH WEIGHT], weight for body: [BODY WEIGHT]". The evaluation uses the treatment plan P and the clinical goals g using an LLM:

To further improve the LLM's capability to understand the relationship between the importance weights θ and the resulting plan P from the inner-loop optimizer, we provide a set of paired plans and their corresponding importance weights P θ {( , )} i i i N =1 as in-context examples for TGD. To evaluate a treatment plan, we adopt several commonly used metrics. We consider the mean dose delivered to the target/organ volume, as well as Dq, which denotes the minimum dose received by q% of the target/organ volume.

elements.label: text
elements.text: First, we show that the textual gradients generated by TextGrad provide meaningful feedback for this problem. As shown in Fig. 3a, when there is dose spillage outside the PTV, the textual gradient suggests an increase in the importance weight for the PTV. This adjustment results in a more uniform and confined dose for the PTV. However, this can lead to insufficient protection of the bladder and rectum as their relative weights are reduced. Therefore, in the following step, the feedback suggests slightly increasing the weights for the bladder and rectum, resulting in better protection (Fig. 3b,c).

elements.label: text
elements.text: We compared TextGrad-optimized plans with clinically approved plans used to treat five patients with prostate cancer. Although automated planning systems exist 36-39 , they have yet to become standard practice and cannot be used as a reliable source of ground truth. Therefore, manually designed and clinically approved plans continue to serve as the gold standard. In Fig. 3d, we assess TextGrad's capabilities in achieving clinical goals for the PTV region. TextGrad outperforms clinical plans, achieving a higher mean dose, and a D95 that exactly matches the prescribed dose, where D95 denotes the minimum dose received by 95% of the target/organ volume. In Fig. 3e, we focus on the protection of healthy organs. TextGrad-optimized plans achieve lower mean doses for these healthy organs, suggesting better organ protection than human-optimized plans. Overall, these results are presented as an illustrative demonstration of TextGrad's potential rather than a definitive statement on clinical effectiveness. In Extended Data Fig. 6, we show that TextGrad also outperforms a Bayesian optimization algorithm, and give further details in Methods.

elements.label: section_header
elements.text: Optimizing compound AI systems

elements.label: text
elements.text: Finally, we investigate the ability of TextGrad to optimize compound AI systems involving multiple variables and longer chains of reasoning.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Our first study focuses on Chameleon 40 , a sophisticated agentic system with multiple LLM modules using diverse tools. Chameleon integrates various tools to tackle a broad range of tasks, leveraging abilities such as visual perception and knowledge retrieval. However, its original planning and execution pipeline is static with no feedback mechanism, which can lead to error accumulation as the steps progress.

elements.label: text
elements.text: To address this, we use TextGrad to optimize the solution steps provided by Chameleon. This process starts with a standard forward pass through all modules. Subsequently, it iteratively optimizes each module's output, starting from the first module and progressing to the last. For each module, the optimization process evaluates the final response using a loss function, computes gradients via TextGrad and backpropagates these gradients to update the module's output. By introducing this feedback loop, we address the limitations of static execution in the original Chameleon system. We evaluate this approach using ScienceQA-IMG, which requires the coordination of multiple tools in visual perception and knowledge retrieval (Supplementary Note 9).

elements.label: text
elements.text: The results in Fig. 4 show the effectiveness of TextGrad in optimizing Chameleon. Through the identification of errors in reasoning traces and iterative backpropagation of textual gradients to refine module outputs (as shown in Fig. 4a,b), TextGrad achieves a 5.7% increase over the baseline performance with 2 optimization iterations, and a 7.7% gain with 3 iterations (Fig. 4e). These findings highlight the potential of TextGrad to enhance compound systems like Chameleon.

elements.label: text
elements.text: In our second study, we use TextGrad to improve the spatial reasoning ability of multimodal models. elements.text: Discussion

elements.label: text
elements.text: TextGrad is built on three principles: (1) it is a general and performant framework that is not handcrafted for a specific application domain; (2) it is easy to use, mirroring PyTorch abstractions, thus allowing knowledge transfer; and (3) it is fully open source. Through TextGrad, we obtained state-of-the-art results in code optimization and PhD-level question answering, optimized prompts, and provided proof-of-concept results in optimizing molecules and treatment plans.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Previous studies have explored using LLMs as optimizers for prompt engineering and self-improvement 5,23,31 . Although these frameworks demonstrated the capabilities of LLMs in specific domains such as prompt optimization, our work introduces a general framework based uniquely on backpropagating natural language feedback that extends beyond prompts to optimize diverse components including code, molecules and treatment plans.

elements.label: text
elements.text: There are various limitations that motivate future work to realize the potential of optimization frameworks powered by LLMs. We hope that TextGrad can be used to accelerate iterative processes in scientific discovery and increase the productivity of engineering efforts. Second, there is a large design space for algorithms to backpropagate textual feedback. We believe that there are many connections to be drawn between numerical optimization, automatic differentiation and TextGrad. Finally, although we conducted proof-of-concept applications of TextGrad to design molecules and treatment plans with in silico validations, the ultimate test requires experimental and clinical assessments, which are outside of the scope of this paper.

elements.label: text
elements.text: As AI systems shift from training individual models to optimizing compound systems with multiple interacting LLM components and tools, we need a new generation of optimizers. TextGrad combines the reasoning power of LLMs with the decomposable efficiency of backpropagation to create a general framework to optimize AI systems.

elements.label: section_header
elements.text: Code optimization

elements.label: text
elements.text: Reflexion is the state-of-the-art method on the LeetCode Hard dataset. Their approach prompts an LLM to self-reflect on code snippets and the errors that were generated at test time using candidate unit tests. Given the self-reflection, the LLM is prompted again to provide an updated piece of code, conditioned on the self-reflection and the errors. We ran Reflexion on LeetCode Hard using gpt-4o using one in-context demonstration to guide the behaviour (one shot). In addition to Reflexion, we also run a zero-shot baseline using gpt-4o mimicking the same zero-shot baseline described in the Reflexion paper. In contrast to Reflexion, TextGrad runs in a zero-shot setting, without any demonstrations. In Extended Data Fig. 3a, we show the code refinement objective used in this paper.

elements.label: text
elements.text: We ran the experiment five times with five different seeds and we averaged the results. At each iteration of optimization, TextGrad makes one call to gpt-4o to evaluate the test-time loss, one call to collect textual gradients and one call to update the code snippet. The number of coding problems in LeetCode Hard is 39.

elements.label: section_header
elements.text: Solution optimization

elements.label: text
elements.text: The objective function for the refinement can be found in Extended Data Fig. 4b. Similarly, we report the objective used for multimodal solution optimization in Supplementary Note 4.

elements.label: text
elements.text: GPQA is a recent benchmark where challenging multiple-choice questions in physics, biology and chemistry are created and labelled by domain experts who have or are pursuing PhD degrees. In this benchmark, experts and skilled non-experts are reported to achieve 81% and 22% accuracy, respectively, demonstrating the difficulty of the questions. We also use two challenging subsets (machine learning and college physics) of the MMLU question-answering benchmark that is used to track the progress of language modelling and whether LLMs reached human-level performance. Here the expert human accuracy on average is around 90%.

elements.label: text
elements.text: We further test solution optimization in multimodal problems, specifically the MathVista and ScienceQA tasks. MathVista is a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating models' capabilities in mathematical reasoning with visual contexts. It contains seven mathematical reasoning categories including arithmetic reasoning, algebraic reasoning and statistical reasoning, and requires fine-grained visual understanding across natural images, diagrams, charts and graphs. We utilize the testmini split with 1,000 examples for evaluation. ScienceQA is a multimodal benchmark of multiple-choice questions in scientific domains. It covers three subjects: nature science, social science and language science, featuring a diverse set of domains and topics. We conduct experiments on ScienceQA-IMG, the test split in multimodal setting, which consists of 2,017 examples. We provide further details on format and prompts in Supplementary Note 4.

elements.label: text
elements.text: We report three baselines. First, the reported results in the gpt-4o release document states 53.6% accuracy. However, their official implementation uses a temperature of 0.5 for generations, thus we also test gpt-4o with temperature 0 and chain of thought (CoT) prompting provided in the official implementation. For TextGrad, we perform three iterations of test-time updates (that is, update the solution three times) and perform majority voting across all solutions to get the final answer. We use string-based metrics to compute the final accuracy of each answer. Finally, we report Reflexion as another baseline, where we also run their algorithm with three iterations (that is, update the answer three times) and perform majority voting across all solutions to get the final answer.

elements.label: section_header
elements.text: Prompt optimization

elements.label: text
elements.text: Here, we use TextGrad in a minibatch stochastic gradient descent setting 43 . In particular, at each iteration, we use a few training examples for training. A pseudocode and short implementation can be found in the snippet above. Full details of prompt optimization can be found in Supplementary Note 5.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Furthermore, we can decompose a prompt into an instruction and in-context demonstrations, and apply the same strategy to optimize them jointly using textual gradients. For instance, we can initialize the in-context demonstrations using input-output samples from the training dataset, then optimize them using TGD.

elements.label: text
elements.text: We explore improving the performance of gpt-3.5-turbo using gpt-4o to provide feedback during backpropagation. In particular, although the forward model that performs the reasoning is gpt-3.5-turbo, we use gpt-4o to provide the feedback and improve the prompt. We use a batch size of 3 with 12 iterations, that is, the model sees 36 training examples in total, sampled randomly with replacement. After each iteration, we run a validation loop with the validation set of the datasets,

elements.label: text
elements.text: and if the performance is better than the previous iteration we update the prompt, which consists of a separate instruction variable, and the in-context demonstrations.

elements.label: text
elements.text: We explore prompt optimization in multiple datasets, including the two standard reasoning tasks (object counting and word sorting) from Big Bench Hard (randomly split into 51/100/99 train/validation/ test samples) and GSM8k grade-school maths problem solving (using train/validation/test splits from DSPy). For GSM8k and object counting, we use a string-based exact match metric to quantify accuracy (that is, whether the final number provided in the response is the same as the ground-truth answer). For word sorting, we use an LLM to compare the response and the ground-truth answer. We give more details about the tasks, prompts and example queries in Supplementary Note 5.1.

elements.label: text
elements.text: We have three main baselines:

elements.label: list_item
elements.text: Zero-shot CoT. We initialize all prompts as a zero-shot CoT prompt, where a model is instructed to 'Think step by step' to explain its reasoning before giving its answer. This strategy is well known to be a strong baseline for prompting.

elements.label: list_item
elements.text: DSPy is a state-of-the-art language model programming and prompt optimization framework; thus we use it as the reference baseline. We instantiate DSPy's BootstrappedFewShotRandomSearch optimizer with ten candidate programs and eight few-shot examples. This optimizer identifies demonstrations to include in the prompt as few-shot examples. This selection is done through generating traces of LLM inputs and outputs that individually pass the metric (in this case, accuracy) and includes CoT reasoning. DSPy then app­ lies random search over subsets of up to size eight shots with these demonstrations.

elements.label: list_item
elements.text: OPRO is one of the first methods to use LLMs as optimizers, where given a set of prompts and their performance, an optimizer LLM generates new candidate prompts. We use all of the hyperparameters as reported in the paper. At each iteration OPRO generates 8 candidate prompts by prompting the optimizer LLM with 20 best-performing prompts along with their performance, and 3 exemplars from the dataset. We perform eight iterations of this procedure.

elements.label: section_header
elements.text: Treatment planning

elements.label: text
elements.text: The dataset used in this study comprised imaging and treatment plans for five patients with prostate cancer who underwent intensity-modulated radiation therapy. The available data for each patient includes computed tomography scans, delineated anatomical structures and clinically approved treatment plans obtained via Eclipse.

elements.label: text
elements.text: As we mentioned in the results, TextGrad is used to optimize the hyperparameters (for example, importance weights for PTV and OARs) of the inner-loop numerical optimizer that generates the treatment plan. This optimization is done using a variation of TextGrad, that is, 'projected gradient descent with momentum updates'. In particular, three prostate cancer treatment plans optimized by clinicians, along with their corresponding hyperparameters, are provided as in-context examples. These examples guide the updates of the hyperparameters. Moreover, the historical hyperparameters and the textual gradients from past iterations, as an analogy to momentum, are also included in the prompts for updating the hyperparameters. This additional context helps refine the optimization process. The optimization will be stopped if the loss suggests all protocols meet, otherwise, it will be stopped if the maximum number of iterations (we set it to ten) is reached.

elements.label: text
elements.text: The importance weights are all initialized at 100 for different organs. The dose objectives are set to 70.20 for PTV, 0.00 for bladder and rectum, and 30.00 for femoral heads and body, and fixed during optimization.

elements.label: text
elements.text: To evaluate a treatment plan, we adopt several frequently used dose metrics, as a plan cannot be evaluated using a single metric. We consider the mean dose delivered to the target/organ volume, as well as Dq, which denotes the minimum dose received by q% of the target/organ volume.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Throughout our experiments, we compare the plans generated by TextGrad with multiple baselines. Our first baseline uses plans generated by certified physicists from our institution with multiple years of experience in developing treatment plans across various cancer types. Our second baseline uses plans produced using Bayesian optimization, which optimizes hyperparameters θ (for example, importance weights for PTV and OARs) by employing a weighted sum of multiple plan evaluation metrics 44 as the objective function. Specifically, the objective is defined as

elements.label: text
elements.text: where mi represents the plan evaluation metric derived from the generated plan with hyperparameter θ, and mi denotes the corresponding clinical goal. The term pi indicates the rank of importance for each plan evaluation metric.

elements.label: text
elements.text: For PTV, we use the mean dose and D95 as evaluation metrics with m =70.20, assigning them an importance rank p of 1. For the OARs, that is, bladder and rectum, we consider the mean dose, D5, and D50 with m =0.00, and an importance rank p of 2.

elements.label: text
elements.text: We implement Bayesian optimization using Optuna 45 . The number of optimization trials in Optuna is set to 50. For all hyperparameters, we configure the suggest_float range to [100, 400], while leaving the remaining parameters as default.

elements.label: text
elements.text: In Extended Data Fig. 6, we show additional results on comparing TextGrad-optimized plan with clinicians optimized plans. Although Bayesian optimization can optimize the plan quality metric (PQM) score function, it produces significantly worse results, particularly in terms of dose conformity, and converges slowly, typically requiring an average of 21.3 iterations. In contrast, our method, TextGrad, generates high-quality plans in just ten iterations. The results illustrate the effectiveness of TextGrad in guiding iterative improvements in optimization but do not constitute a direct evaluation of clinical utility.

elements.label: section_header
elements.text: Optimizing compound AI systems

elements.label: text
elements.text: Optimizing the Chameleon agentic system. The original Chameleon system is described in Algorithm 2 (Supplementary Note 9). It consists of a planner P and a module inventory of tools M. Given an input query q, the planner generates a plan p q ← ( ; ) P M that specifies a sequence of modules to execute. Executing the plan starts from an empty cache c =∅ 0 . At each step t, the chosen module M t is run as y t ← M t (q; c t-1 ), after which the cache is updated: c t ← update_cache(c t-1 , y t ). After all T steps, the final response is r = y T .

elements.label: text
elements.text: We augment this procedure, as shown in Algorithm 3 (Supplementary Note 9), by introducing textual gradient-based optimization. After an initial forward pass, we iteratively refine each module's output. We quantify the final response quality via a loss function L, compute textual gradients using TextGrad and propagate these gradients back to earlier steps in the chain, adjusting their outputs accordingly. This iterative process gradually improves the intermediate reasoning steps and, consequently, the final answer. We evaluate the original and TextGrad-optimized systems on ScienceQA-IMG and experiment with two and three optimization iterations to study the impact of iteration count. Details are available at Supplementary Note 9.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Improving spatial reasoning ability by jointly optimizing prompts and solutions. We apply TextGrad to improve spatial reasoning ability on the visual question-answering task. In visual question answering, instructional prompts are used to guide the model in answering the questions following. We further compute the objective in TextGrad by prompting a language model and treating both the prompts embedded in the loss function and the instructional prompts as variables to be optimized. The generated solutions to the questions are optimized together.

elements.label: text
elements.text: We split the HQH dataset into 70/30/100 (train/validation/test) splits, out of the 200 samples in the relation question type. The complete optimization process is as follows. We first warm up the optimization process where the instructions to the language model that specify the task, and the instructions for the loss function used to evaluate generated answers are optimized in an alternating fashion with a batch size set to ten (in total seven iterations). We use the prompts that achieve the best validation accuracy for test-time optimization. At test time, each solution is optimized for three iterations (that is, update the solution three times). Majority voting across all solutions is performed to get the final answer.

elements.label: section_header
elements.text: Molecule optimization

elements.label: text
elements.text: As a proof of concept, we also explore TextGrad's applications to molecular optimization, and demonstrate how our framework can be used to interface with domain-specific tools in scientific tasks (Supplementary Note 8).

elements.label: text
elements.text: We optimize chemical molecules encoded as text (simplified molecular input line entry system (SMILES) strings) with respect to one or several molecular scoring functions. We restrict our scoring functions to in silico methods, namely, Autodock Vina, which measures the binding affinity of a molecule against a target protein, and quantitative estimate of drug-likeness (QED), which measures how 'druglike' a molecule is. We initialize a molecule as a small starting fragment, and perform several iterations of optimization using TGD. At each iteration, the loss is constructed by concatenating each score into a single 'textual' loss.

elements.label: text
elements.text: We evaluate our methods using two baselines: (1) molecular characteristics of approved drugs against a matched set of protein targets (Extended Data Fig. 1); and (2) oracle efficiency compared with state-of-the-art molecular optimization algorithms (Extended Data Fig. 2). We observe that TextGrad produces molecules with a similar distribution to its clinical counterparts across both optimized and non-optimized molecular properties, but with low structural similarity to approved drugs or existing compounds. Compared with state-of-the-art molecular optimization algorithms, TextGrad consistently produces higher-performing molecules while using fewer evaluations on a diverse set of protein targets. Although promising, we caution that the practical value of these molecules is limited and should be taken as a proof of concept only. Our evaluations are limited by their reliance on in silico property predictors, which are not accurate substitutes for thorough experimental and clinical evaluation.

elements.label: section_header
elements.text: Supplementary Note 1.1 Variables

elements.label: text
elements.text: Variables are the nodes in the computation graph. Below are the most important attributes of Variables:

elements.label: list_item
elements.text: Value is the unstructured data that the variable contains. Throughout this manuscript, all values are text data.

elements.label: list_item
elements.text: Role description is an informative string that describes the role of the variable in the computation graph. We use these roles to let the user inject knowledge into the graph and guide the optimization behavior. More information is described below.

elements.label: list_item
elements.text: Gradients are the natural language feedback provided by the LLMs during the backward pass. These describe the changes to make the variable so that the downstream loss can be improved. For an example backward operation that populates gradients, please read Supplementary Note 1.3.

elements.label: list_item
elements.text: Predecessors are the set of variables that are used to generate a given variable. For instance, if we are giving an instruction to an LLM and getting a response, the instruction would be the predecessor of the response. During the backward pass, the gradients on the successor are passed to its predecessors, to provide guidance around how to improve the downstream objective.

elements.label: list_item
elements.text: Requires grad indicates whether or not the gradients will be populated during the backward pass, analogous to PyTorch. For instance, if the user does not wish to compute gradients for a question, then simply write Variable(value=question, requires_grad=False, ...) to indicate this.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Role description. In TextGrad, each variable has a role description. In particular, this is a string that describes the role of the variable in the computation graph, such as "system prompt to the language model" or "prediction by the language model" . While sometimes populated automatically, in general role descriptions are one of the primary ways to inject user knowledge into the optimization process.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Empirically, we find that role descriptions can significantly steer the optimization process. For instance, setting the role of a prediction to be "the final numerical answer to the language model" guides the Textual Gradient Descent optimizer, that prompts a language model to update the value of the variable using the feedback, to update the variable such that it is only a numerical value. In comparison, a role description such as "the reasoning for the solution and the final prediction" guides the optimizer to produce the reasoning along with the final prediction.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Here is an example usage:

elements.label: code
elements.text: 1 import textgrad as tg 2 3 system_prompt = tg.Variable("You will be given a question and think step -by-step.", requires_grad=True , role_description="system prompt to the language model that will be reused across queries") 4 5 model = tg.BlackBoxLLM(system_prompt=system_prompt)

elements.label: caption
elements.text: Code Snippet 1 An example usage of a role description.

elements.label: section_header
elements.text: Supplementary Note 1.2 Backpropagation

elements.label: text
elements.text: The backpropagation algorithm in TextGrad mirrors existing autograd frameworks for deep learning. See Algorithm 1 for the pseudocode.

elements.label: section_header
elements.text: Algorithm 1 Backpropagation in TextGrad

elements.label: code
elements.text: 1: Input: Variables v ∈ V in a graph, loss variable L, backward engine (LLM) M that will provide textual gradients 2: # Initializing gradients 3: for each v ∈ V do 4: v.gradients = ∅ 5: end for 6: # Topological Sorting 7: Q⇐TopologicalSort(G) 8: # Backpropagation 9: for v in Q do 10: # Populate gradients in predecessors 11: for each u ∈ PredecessorsOf(v) do 12: # We omit subscript v in f. f is the function that generates v, and ∇f is the backward operation for that function. 13: # Semantically, it provides feedback to the variable u, given how v is produced, and the feedback we already collected for v. 14: u.gradients.add (∇f (u, v, ∂L ∂v )) 15: end for 16: end for

elements.label: section_header
elements.text: Supplementary Note 1.3 Functions

elements.label: text
elements.text: TextGrad offers several operations where both the forward and backward computations are defined - as such, these operations are composable. The abstract textgrad.autograd.Function class has two methods: forward and backward, mirroring the PyTorch syntax. Each function has to define both of these methods. Below, we describe a couple of the most used operations in this paper.

elements.label: text
elements.text: LLMCall function. Currently, the most crucial operation in TextGrad is the call to language models.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Forward mode. The forward mode is simple: We make a call to an LLM, through an API or through the local machine. When a call is made, all the input variables are registered as the predecessors of the response from the LLM. For instance, if we ask a question to an LLM using an instruction and a question variable, the response variable's predecessors will be [instruction, question]. When doing the backward pass, the gradients on the response will be backpropagated to question and instruction.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Backward mode. To ensure the backward function runs smoothly and generally, we add the following glossary to the system prompt:

elements.label: text

elements.label: text

elements.label: text

elements.label: text
elements.text: # - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.

elements.label: text
elements.text: # - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Using these tags, the LLM is made aware of the objective, the role and the value of the variable to give feedback to, and the full conversation in the forward mode.

The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode... ' , 'Adding X can fix this error because... ' , 'Removing X can improve the objective function because... ' , 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ... ' , that gets at the downstream objective.

elements.label: text
elements.text: In TextGrad it is possible use constraints when optimizing variables. These constraints are all defined as natural language descriptions. For example, one can prompt optimizer to update the variable but to conclude its response with an answer during the update:

elements.label: text

elements.label: section_header
elements.text: Supplementary Note 3.1 Methodology

elements.label: text
elements.text: Baseline details. We re-run Reflexion [2] using the code by the authors currently available online. We had to make minor changes to ensure it ran correctly in our setting but we also contacted the original authors and ask feedback on our edits to ensure our evaluation was consistent. Moreover, we had to re-extract the LeetCodeHard [2] dataset using the authors' pipeline; this means that it is likely that the dataset we are using in this manuscript is not the same dataset that was used in the Reflexion paper. While this dataset contains a set of simple tests to check if the code works as expected, the real evaluation in this context is given by passing the tests on the LeetCode platform.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Reflexion is run with a one-shot prompt that is meant to instruct the model on how to provide feedback. The pipeline run by Reflexion is as follows: given in input a prompt to generate code, a language model generates a first solution. If this solution passes the local tests, it is then submitted to the LeetCode platform to be evaluated on harder tests. However, if the solution does not pass the tests, we ask for feedback through Reflexion and optimize the code. Once again, if the new solution passes the local tests, we submit it to the LeetCode platform. We do this optimization for five iterations.

elements.label: section_header
elements.text: Supplementary Note 7.1 Prompts

elements.label: text
elements.text: Radiotherapy treatment plan evaluation can based on various dimensions, therefore there is no single score that can indicate the quality of plans. We adopt LLM to compute the "loss" by prompting it to assess the plan quality with clinical protocols. Specifically, LLM is used to compare each protocol with the current plan and produce the final assessment.

elements.label: section_header
elements.text: Supplementary Note 7.2 Inner-loop optimization for treatment planning

elements.label: text
elements.text: We employ a two-loop optimization approach [16], which includes i) an inner loop for inverse planning and ii) an outer loop for optimizing the hyperparameters of the inner loop. The inner loop focuses on traditional fluence map optimization, seeking to determine the optimal fluence map x by minimizing a cost function that combines multiple weighted objectives for various targets and organs at risk. This cost function is defined as:

elements.label: text
elements.text: Here, {wt}Nt t=1 and {ws}Ns s=1 are the importance weights (the hyperparameters optimized by TextGrad) that balance the various objectives for Nt PTV targets and Ns OARs, respectively. K denotes the dose influence matrix, which specifies the dose per fluence unit delivered to each voxel in the volume by each beamlet. {dt}Nt t=1 and {ds}Ns s=1 are the scalar objective doses for each structure. The cost function essentially penalizes squared deviations from the target objective doses for the PTV targets and penalizes squared overdosing for the OARs only when doses exceed ds. The Heaviside function Θ is used to ensure the objective considers only positive values. The minimization is constrained to positive x values and ensures that D95 - the minimum dose received by 95% of the structure volume - matches the prescribed dose for the clinical goal. We use matRad [17] with interior point algorithms to solve the inner-loop optimization.

elements.label: text
elements.text: In clinical practice, evaluating radiotherapy treatment plans involves balancing multiple quality metrics (e.g., mean dose, D95), without a clear consensus on their relative importance. This complexity makes it difficult to design a unified "score function" that combines these metrics into a single objective for direct optimization. Additionally, many of these metrics are non-differentiable, which complicates the use of gradient-based optimization techniques. As a result, designing an effective optimization algorithm for the outer loop is both challenging and critical for successful automatic radiation oncology treatment planning.

Since some of these metrics are non-differentiable, [18] applied Bayesian Optimization (BO) to optimize the hyperparameters in the outer loop. Following their approach, we use Optuna [19] to implement Bayesian optimization for PQM as our baseline.

elements.label: section_header
elements.text: Supplementary Note 8 Molecule optimization

elements.label: section_header
elements.text: Supplementary Note 8.1 Molecule optimization

elements.label: text
elements.text: TextGrad supports a variety of optimization problems, including multi-objective optimization tasks commonly found in science and engineering applications. For example, in drug discovery, researchers seek to discover or design molecules that maximize a variety of objectives with regards to synthesizability, efficacy, and safety [20, 21]. To demonstrate TextGrad's applications to multi-objective optimization, we apply TextGrad to drug molecule optimization, and show how our framework can interface with computational tools and optimize chemical structures towards simultaneously improving their binding affinity and druglikeness as measured by in silico oracles.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Task. A critical consideration for potential drug molecules is their binding affinity, which represents the strength of the interactions between the molecule and its protein target. Drug designers seek molecules with high binding affinities to relevant drug targets, as they require lower and less frequent doses to achieve efficacy. This affinity can be quantified by free energy ∆G, which describes the ratio of probabilities between bound and unbound ligand-receptor pairs. ∆G can be estimated using "docking" simulations of protein-ligand binding [22, 23]. In our experiments, we employ the Vina score from the Autodock Vina tool, a widely used physics-based docking simulator [24]. A more negative Vina score indicates that the drug is predicted to be more likely to bind to its intended target.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Potential drug molecules are also evaluated by their druglikeness, which estimates how the molecule will behave in vivo, with respect to solubility, permeability, metabolic stability and transporter effects. Molecules with high druglikeness are more likely to be absorbed by the body and reach their targets [25]. One metric for "druglikeness" is the Quantitative Estimate of Druglikeness (QED) score, a weighted composite score of chemical characteristics such as molecular weight, lipophilicity, polar surface area, among others. The QED score ranges from 0 to 1, where 1 indicates high druglikeness [26].

elements.label: text
elements.text: Though there are many more considerations for successful molecules, in our experiments, we restrict our objectives to minimizing the Vina score and maximizing the QED. Since each score evaluates different considerations in molecular design, optimizing one does not necessarily imply improvement in the other. Thus, optimizing molecules that simultaneously improve both objectives is non-trivial.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Methods. We apply TextGrad to drug molecule optimization by encoding molecules as SMILES strings and constructing a multi-objective loss from the Vina and QED scores. Namely, we perform test-time optimization over SMILES strings, where the gradients generated by TextGrad with respect to the multi-objective loss are used to update the text representing the molecule:

elements.label: text
elements.text: Evaluation = LLM((Affinity(SMILESi, target), Druglikeness(SMILESi)),

elements.label: text
elements.text: We use gpt-4o as our LLM with the prompt text found in Supplementary Note 8.3. At each iteration, the current molecule is evaluated by estimating its binding affinity to the target protein using the Vina score from Autodock Vina and using the QED score for druglikeness from RDKit (Supplementary Note 8.2). Each molecule is initialized as a small chemical fragment from a functional group. We apply TextGrad to all 58 targets in the DOCKSTRING molecule evaluation benchmark [27]. These 58 targets consist of clinically relevant proteins sampled from a variety of structural classes, 29 of which have clinically approved drugs. For each target, we optimize a starting fragment using TextGrad for up to 10 iterations (Supplementary Note 8.8), for 3 unique initial fragments. To evaluate our performance, we compare the characteristics of the molecules generated by TextGrad to clinically approved drugs for the respective protein (Supplementary Note 8.4).

elements.label: text
elements.text: Results. For all 58 targets, TextGrad consistently generates molecules with improved binding affinity and druglikeness irrespective of the initial starting fragment (Supplementary Note 8.5). For the 29 protein targets with clinically approved drugs, we observe that TextGrad generates molecules with highly competitive affinity and druglikeness when compared to clinical molecules evaluated using the same loss function (Extended Data Fig. 1b). The resulting molecules exhibit unique structures compared to their clinical approved counterparts and existing compounds (Supplementary Note 8.6), while maintaining similar in silico safety profiles (Supplementary Note 8.7). By combining specialized tools from computational chemistry with the general knowledge and reasoning capabilities of LLMs, TextGrad enables users to perform molecule optimization from arbitrary starting molecules, without the need for additional finetuning datasets, or high-performing initializations from curated compound libraries. Furthermore, TextGrad 's natural language gradients enable users to transparently analyze the optimization process and the impetus for the changes between each molecule in the trajectory. Though promising, we caution that the practical value of the molecules TextGrad has generated are limited. In particular, we optimize over and evaluate only a few properties, all evaluated using in silico objective functions (e.g. Vina, QED, ADMET scores), which are not reliable substitutes for experimental and clinical evaluation.

elements.label: section_header
elements.text: Supplementary Note 8.2 Docking and druglikeness evaluation

elements.label: text
elements.text: To optimize molecules, we evaluate the binding affinity and druglikeness of chemical structures encoded as SMILES strings. To compute both metrics, the generated SMILES string is first converted into an octet-complete Lewis dot structure using RDKit's MolFromSmiles functionality. This method "sanitizes" molecules by adding explicit hydrogens, kekulizing aromatic rings, standardizing valence states, and assigning radicals [28]. If this sanitization process fails at any step, whether through a structural ambiguity or an invalid molecule, the QED and Vina scores are replaced with a single string informing TextGrad that the molecule is invalid.

elements.label: text
elements.text: If the generated SMILES string does represent a valid chemical structure, we compute the QED score using RDKit's Chem.QED function. While QED scores can be quickly and reliably computed, docking scores can vary significantly depending on target and ligand structure preparation. To ensure consistency, we calculate Vina scores using the DOCKSTRING package [27], which implements a standardized docking workflow and provides a set of gold-standard targets. In particular, after the ligand has been sanitized by RDKit, DOCKSTRING (de)-protonates it at pH 7.4 using Open Babel, and prepares and refines the 3D geometric structure using the Euclidean distance geometry algorithm ETKG and the classical force field MMFF94. Finally, Gasteiger charges are computed for all ligand atoms, and the resulting structure is saved as a ligand PDBQT file passed to Autodock Vina. For target preparation, the DOCKSTRING benchmark suite provides 58 curated crystal structures of clinically relevant proteins, with the majority at less than 2.5 Å resolution. These structures are specially prepared to improve correlations between theoretical and experimental binding affinities, for example by manual addition of polar hydrogens and removal of residual water and solute molecules. DOCKSTRING also standardizes simulation parameters such as numerical seeds, search box coordinates, and sampling exhausitivity, to ensure reproducible scoring.

elements.label: text
elements.text: In practice, drug efficacy is typically a higher priority than absorbtion efficiency [29, 30], so we set the vina_qed_ratio to be 10. Empirically, we observe that by scaling this prioritization factor, we can tune TextGrad's generation towards molecules with differing binding affinity and druglikness tradeoffs (Supplementary Note 8.9). This prioritization also allows us to simplify post-hoc selection and ranking of the generated molecules with a single "overall" score defined as follows, where a lower overall score soverall indicates a better molecule:

elements.text: Since the QED score is bounded between 0 and 1, and the Vina score typically ranges between -3.0 to -12.0 kcal/mol, soverall with the default vina_qed_ratio = 10 places approximately 10 times more emphasis on binding affinity than druglikeness as desired.

elements.label: section_header
elements.text: Supplementary Note 8.4 Benchmarks

elements.label: text
elements.text: To benchmark the performance of TextGrad generated molecules, we compare their characteristics to clinically approved drugs for the same protein targets found in DrugBank, a database of 16, 619 drugs [31]. To ensure that the DrugBank molecules were both comparable and high quality, we filtered for drugs that were small molecules, had full clinical approval, and were designed for orthosteric binding with the same active site in the DOCKSTRING benchmark suite. After these filtering criteria, we identified 118 drugs targeting 29 of the 58 DOCKSTRING proteins. When evaluating binding affinity and druglikeness for the clinically approved drugs, we compute the Vina and QED scores using the same tools and workflow described in Supplementary Note 8.2, exactly as applied to the TextGrad molecules.

elements.label: section_header
elements.text: Supplementary Note 8.5 Initialization

elements.label: text
elements.text: In practice, molecular optimization is typically accelerated by large scale preoptimization screening, where libraries of millions or even billions of existing chemical structures are scored and ranked by docking, druglikeness, and other metrics. Only the most promising structures, termed "leads" , are further refined by medicinal chemists [32]. While TextGrad is capable of optimizing any initial molecule, in this work, we instead select our three initial molecules from simple fragments of common functional groups, shown in Supplementary Fig. 2 in order to more accurately characterize it's performance and avoid biasing its designs towards existing drugs. These fragments are highly diverse, and belong to different functional groups. Although these initial fragments have differing druglikness and binding affinity characteristics, the impact of the starting fragment on TextGrad's performance is minimal, and TextGrad is capable of generating molecules with high druglikeness and binding affinity from all three fragments.

elements.label: section_header
elements.text: Supplementary Note 8.6 Chemical novelty

elements.label: text
elements.text: One of the primary concerns with using LLM models in scientific discovery is their capacity to simply memorize and regurgitate their training sets instead of performing logical reasoning [33]. Since recent models like gpt-4o are trained on massive, opaque datasets, a key concern is that the molecules TextGrad generates may simply be duplicates of clinically approved molecules for their respective targets. To quantify and test the extent or existence of this "memorization" effect, we compare the molecules that TextGrad generates with approved drugs for their respective protein targets, as well as unrelated but existing druglike chemical compounds.

elements.label: text
elements.text: We first compare TextGrad generated molecules for a particular protein target with all the clinically approved small molecules found in Drugbank for the same target (see Supplementary Note 8.4 for filtering criteria) using the Tversky similarity score on RDKit daylight chemical fingerprints. The Tversky similarity score is not symmetric, and compares substructures between a variant and reference molecule [34]. In our application, this is preferred as it assigns a high score to generated (variant) molecules that contain most or all of the substructures in the Drugbank (reference) molecule, even if there exist other extraneous substructures in the generated molecule that reduce the symmetric overlap between the two molecules. A Tversky score of 1.0 indicates that the TextGrad molecule is a complete subset of the Drugbank molecule, while 0.0 indicates no overlap.

elements.label: caption
elements.text: Supplementary Fig. 3 Structural novelty. (a) We observe increasing novelty over optimization updates, where a generated molecule is considered"novel" if there does not exist any existing molecule in ChEMBL with a Tanimoto similarity score greater than 0.8. (b,c,d) We estimate substructure similarity using the Tversky metric between TextGrad molecules and clinically approved drugs for each target. While there are a wide range of similarity scores, we observe that similarity with known drugs has little correlation with molecule performance, suggesting that TextGrad's generation process is weakly influenced by "memorized" knowledge of clinically approved structures.

elements.label: text
elements.text: In order to analyze the most relevant chemical structures, we restricted our analysis to a set of high performing TextGrad molecules, rather than all molecules from all iterations. In particular, using the overall score described in Equation H10, we selected the best molecule for each protein target and for each initial fragment, for a total of 87 generated molecules (29 druggable targets x 3 initial fragments) and 118 clinically approved drugs across 29 targets. For each target, we compute all pairwise Tversky scores between the 3 TextGrad molecules and the Drugbank molecules approved for that target, setting the Drugbank molecule as the reference, and the TextGrad molecule as the variant.

elements.label: text
elements.text: We observed that the distribution of Tversky similarity scores was quite broad, with a median of 0.42 but ranging from 0.14 to 0.90 (Supplementary Fig. 3b). However, we observe that Tversky similarity between TextGrad and DrugBnak molecules is actually slightly anti-correlated with molecule performance as measured by the overall score, suggesting that TextGrad 's optimization procedure is at best weakly influenced by prior knowledge of approved drugs. In fact, for a variety of generated molecules along a gradient of similarity scores, the generated molecules exhibit QED and Vina scores that match or even exceed their DrugBank counterparts (Supplementary Fig. 3d). We caution however that this does not imply that the TextGrad molecule holds clinical value, as clinically approved molecules are optimized on far more criteria, and our metrics of binding afinity and druglikeness are computed by in silico oracles that may not reflect experimental behavior.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Beyond the similarity to known drugs, we are also interested in observing if TextGrad is generating novel molecules, or discovering previously unknown properties in existing compounds, for example a strong binding affinity to a protein target in a compound that has not been associated with the protein. To answer this question, we perform a Tanimoto similarity search across all of ChEMBL, a manually curated database of 2.4 million bioactive molecules with drug-like properties [35]. Unlike the Tversky score, the Tanimoto metric measures the symetric overlap between two chemical structures, where 1.0 indicates an exact match, and 0.0 no overlap. We classify a TextGrad compound as novel if and only if there does not exist any molecule in ChEMBL with a with a Tanimoto similarity score over 0.80.

elements.label: text
elements.text: While the starting fragments are known molecules, we observe that as the number of iterations increases, TextGrad generates molecules that are progressively less likely to be previously known compounds. By the 6th iteration, 95% of all the molecules generated by TextGrad across all 58 targets and three starting fragments are novel using the criteria above (Supplementary Fig. 3a). By observing the trajectories of generated molecules and analyzing the textual gradients, we hypothesize that the feedback provided by the Vina and QED scores encourages TextGrad to explore chemical space beyond known molecules by progressively adding and removing combinations of functional groups. Since these chemical updates can form a combinatorial number of unique structures, it is reasonable that TextGrad would reach previously unexplored regions of chemical space in a relatively small number of iterations.

elements.label: section_header
elements.text: Supplementary Note 8.7 Extended post-generation analysis

elements.label: text
elements.text: We further evaluate our generated molecules post-generation, focusing on safety profiles related to mutagenisis and clinical toxicity. Mutagenicity refers to the ability of a drug to induce genetic alterations, which may lead to DNA damage and harmful longterm affects. Clinical toxicity refers to a broad range of adverse short or long-term side effects. Importantly, neither druglikeness nor binding affinity are strongly correlated with these criteria, and thus these desirability metrics are not directly optimized or otherwise explicitly encoded in TextGrad's objectives.

elements.label: text
elements.text: To evaluate the propensity for mutagenisis and clinical toxicity, we employ the ADMET-AI model, that predicts these scores from the chemical structures of molecules [36]. ADMET-AI employs a deep learning model trained on multiple relevant datasets. In particular, for mutagenicity, ADMET-AI is trained on 7, 255 drugs from the Ames dataset, a bacterial reverse mutation assay for rapidly screening large numbers of compounds for can induced genetic damage and frameshift mutations. elements.label: section_header
elements.text: Supplementary Note 8.8 Parameter selection and early stopping

elements.label: text
elements.text: In the experiments outlined in Supplementary Note 8.1, we employed early stopping to determine the number of optimization iterations. In particular, we score each molecule produced using a scoring function, and if the mean of the top-K = 5 scores does not improve by more than TOL = 0.1 for more than patience = 5 iterations, the run is terminated, or until the max_epoch = 10 is reached. Since our objective is both Vina and QED optimization, we use the overall score function defined in Equation H10. In general, a higher value of all the parameters (except TOL) will allow for longer explorations, and we invite users to select these parameters to suit their optimization budgets.

elements.label: section_header
elements.text: Supplementary Note 8.9 Multi-objective steerability

elements.label: text
elements.text: We perform additional experiments quantifying the affect of the vina_qed_ratio parameter in steering molecule property distributions in our multi-objective optimization experiment.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Using the prompt provided in Supplementary Note 8.3, we set the vina_qed_ratio to 50, 25, and 1, respectively. This sequence of values represents an increase in the prioritization of the QED score relative to the Vina. Intuitively, for the value of 50, we essentially instruct TextGrad to disregard the QED score, while at 1, we inform TextGrad that the QED and Vina objectives are equally important. Starting from pentane, we optimize molecules for 10 iterations against all 58 proteins in the DOCKSTRING benchmark, for a total of 58 unique trajectories and 580 molecules.

elements.label: text
elements.text: We observe that tuning the vina_qed_ratio alters the distributions of the generated molecules and that an increase in QED prioritization led to a corresponding increase QED values. Conversely, a decrease in Vina prioritization led to a decrease in Vina performance (e.g. higher Vina scores). Using a paired t-test, we observed that the changes in both Vina and QED were statistically significant between the parameter settings of 50 and 1.

elements.text: Supplementary Note 8.10 Gradient specificity analysis

elements.label: text
elements.text: We perform experiments to quantify the information content and specificity of TextGrad gradients. Concretely, we compare two optimization trajectories.

elements.label: list_item
elements.text: Original. In the original TextGrad framework, an initial molecule is modified by computing the loss function against a particular protein and updating its structure based on the gradient computed with respect to the loss. This process is repeated for multiple iterations, with the all gradients computed against the same protein.

elements.label: list_item
elements.text: Random. In the random framework, an initial molecule is modified by randomly selecting a gradient from a different molecule docked against a different protein. This process is repeated for the same number of iterations, but with random gradients selected at each iteration.

elements.label: text
elements.text: We evaluate both sequences of molecules using the loss function (QED and Vina Score) against the original protein. If the gradients produced by TextGrad are nontarget specific, we expect that the randomized trajectory to perform as well as the original trajectory.

elements.label: text
elements.text: We compute "original" trajectories for all 58 targets in the DOCKSTRING benchmark, each starting from three initial starting fragments (benzene, pentane, acetamide) for a total of 174 original trajectories. For each original trajectory, we generate 10 random trajectories using the same initial fragment and evaluated against the same target, for a total of 1, 740 random trajectories. Each trajectory, both random and original, was optimized for 10 iterations. While the optimization length was fixed to allow for a comprehensive comparison across multiple targets and for multiple randomizations, we observed that the trends for both the random and original trajectories are readily apparent within 10 iterations.

elements.label: text
elements.text: We observe that random trajectory produces lower performing molecules relative to original trajectory across both QED and Vina metrics. Using a paired t-test across protein targets and initial molecules, we compute the difference between the QED of the final molecule generated in the original trajectory and the mean QED value of the final molecules across the 10 repetitions in the random trajectories. For a total of n = 174 paired trajectory comparisons, we report that the random trajectories have statistically significant lower QED scores than the original trajectories with a p-value of less than 1e-4. We repeat this comparison for the Vina score, and report similar results, with the random trajectories having significantly higher (worse) Vina scores (p < 1e-4). We also observe that random trajectories have a higher incidence of invalid molecules, producing on aggregate 1.5x more invalid SMILES strings than the original trajectory. Using the same statistical procedure for invalidity as the Vina and QED comparison, we report that the significance is p < 1e-2.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Implementations were taken from the Practical Molecular Optimization (PMO) benchmark suite [39] without modification and with default hyperparameters, with the exception of the Graph MCTS algorithm which accepts an initial molecule (default CC). For Graph MCTS, we replaced the default initial molecule with the same molecule used by TextGrad (pentane, acetamide, or benzene). For a full treatment of their implementation and algorithmic details, we refer the reader to the PMO benchmark and their original publications.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Objective. For this comparison, we modified our original multi-objective of optimizing both the Vina and QED scores to only the Vina score since the benchmark algorithms above only accept single-value objective functions. While it is possible to convert our original task of multi-objective Vina/QED optimization into a weighted single-value objective, we elected to simplify the comparison between algorithms and avoid having to arbitrarily select the QED importance factor.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Evaluation metrics. To compare the performances of different molecular optimization algorithms, we use the scaled AUC top-K metric introduced by the Practical Molecular Optimization benchmark [39], with K = 5. Briefly, the top-K trajectory measures the mean performance of the top K molecules generated at for a given oracle budget (in our setting, number of docking simulations). This is preferred over a single "best" (K = 1) molecule as it rewards algorithms that generate multiple viable candidates. The AUC of the top-K trajectory quantifies both the performance of the molecules generated as well the sample efficiency of the algorithm. In our setting, the objective function is the negative docking score (e.g. maximization) which is an unbounded objective that is variable between proteins. In order to compare algorithm performance across multiple proteins, we scale each trajectory to a [0, 1] range by empirically deriving maximal and minimal AUCs for each protein across the set of algorithms compared. Specifically, for a given protein, we set the maximum AUC Top-K to be the AUC if the highest point in the top-K trajectory across all algorithms was discovered at the first oracle call, while the minimum to be the AUC if the lowest point in the top-k trajectory of all algorithms persisted for all oracle calls.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Set-up. We evaluated the 6 benchmark algorithms and TextGrad over all 58 unique protein targets in the DOCKSTRING benchmark dataset. For each protein target and algorithm, we repeated the optimization run three times for different randomization seeds for REINVENT, REINVENT-Selfies, Graph GA, Smiles GA, and GP BO. In the case of TextGrad and Graph MCTS, the runs were repeated for different initial molecules (benzene, pentane, acetamide). Each run was performed for a maximum oracle budget (e.g. number of docking simulations) of 50. For the benchmark algorithms, we ran all trajectories for the full 50 oracle calls. For TextGrad, in order to limit the number of LLM calls, we employed the early stopping procedure outlined previously. Briefly, if the mean top-K = 5 objective did not improve by more than TOL = 0.1 for more than patience = 5 iterations, the run was terminated. To calculate the AUC of these early stopped runs, we simply extend the last mean top-K objective score for the remaining oracle calls. Since the mean top-K is a non-decreasing function, this prevents us from overestimating TextGrad's performance. In total, this experiment performed a comprehensive evaluation between the

elements.text: 7 algorithms across 58 proteins with 174 trajectories, and generating a total of 8, 700 molecules.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Results. We outline the performance results across all 58 proteins in Extended Data Fig. 2a and sample trajectories in Extended Data Fig. 2b. We conducted a paired t-test between the AUC Top-K of TextGrad for each protein against all other methods. The difference between TextGrad and all other methods was significant, with the greatest difference between TextGrad and Graph MCTCS and the closest between TextGrad and Graph GA. While these results demonstrate the promising potential of TextGrad to optimize molecules, we do not claim that TextGrad is the best method for this particular task, and have included these comparisons as a proofof-concept. Furthermore, we reiterate that the practical value of TextGrad molecules is limited due to our reliance on in silico evaluation, and should not be interpreted as clinically useful.
